articles.title: Engavetamento deixa quatro feridos em rodovia do litoral de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu na Rodovia Padre Manoel da Nóbrega (SP-055), em Mongaguá (SP). Vítimas sofreram ferimentos leves.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu na Rodovia Padre Manoel da Nóbrega (SP-055), em Mongaguá (SP). Vítimas sofreram ferimentos leves.
articles.body:
Engavetamento deixou quatro feridos e provocou tombamento em Mongaguá (SP). — Foto: Divulgação/Artesp

Um engavetamento envolvendo três carros deixou quatro pessoas feridas na Rodovia Padre Manoel da Nóbrega (SP-055), em Mongaguá , no litoral de São Paulo, nesta sexta-feira (30). Segundo a concessionária Novo Litoral, responsável pelo trecho, um dos veículos tombou na pista após a colisão.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 10h, na altura do km 303, no sentido leste da rodovia. De acordo com a concessionária, o motorista de um dos carros não percebeu que o trânsito estava lento à frente e bateu na traseira de outro veículo, que foi projetado contra um terceiro.

Na sequência, o motorista do primeiro carro perdeu o controle da direção, bateu contra a mureta de proteção e tombou na via. As quatro vítimas tiveram ferimentos leves. Segundo a concessionária, todas assinaram um termo de recusa de remoção pela ambulância.

Todas as faixas e o acostamento da pista leste foram interditados até as 11h07. Durante o atendimento, o tráfego foi desviado para a pista marginal.

Após a liberação das faixas, o trecho ainda registrava congestionamento de aproximadamente 3 quilômetros.

articles.title: Meet Ayaan Wadhwa, the 17-year-old Mumbai student who realised his family’s cook had no safety net after years of work, he then ran workshops that registered 750 domestic workers for government benefits they never knew about
articles.summary: Every day, thousands of domestic workers enter apartment buildings across Mumbai to cook, clean and take care of household chores.
articles.body: Every day, thousands of domestic workers enter apartment buildings across Mumbai to cook, clean and take care of household chores. Yet, while the families they work for may have health insurance, savings and other financial safeguards, many of these workers have little or no access to such security. For 17-year-old Ayaan Wadhwa, the disparity became difficult to ignore after an incident involving a woman who worked at his home. What followed was an initiative that has now helped more than 750 unorganised-sector workers register for government welfare schemes.The idea did not begin with a large campaign or an ambitious social project. It started with a question that stayed with him.A request for financial help that made him thinkThe turning point came when a woman working in the Wadhwa household needed money because her mother was unwell. With no savings or insurance to fall back on, she approached Ayaan's mother, Pinky Panjwani, for a loan.While such situations are not uncommon in many households, the incident prompted Ayaan to think about what would happen to workers who had nobody to turn to."I just kept thinking if we didn’t give it to her, what would she have done?" he recalled in an interview with d2d Youth Story.He began comparing the financial security available to people around him with the circumstances of domestic workers."People around me have medical insurance, and that’s when I realised that most workers don’t have access to something that basic," he says.Ayaan started researching government welfare provisions for workers in the unorganised sector. During this process, he came across the e-Shram portal, a government initiative aimed at registering unorganised-sector workers and connecting them with social security benefits.What surprised him was that the woman who had worked in his household for years had never heard of these provisions.For Ayaan, the problem was not simply the absence of welfare schemes. It was also the lack of awareness about how to access them.From researching schemes to conducting workshopsAyaan's mother, Pinky Panjwani, says his decision to take up the issue developed gradually."It wasn’t a sudden revelation. It was gradual curiosity. He started asking questions, then researching. Then one day, he said he wanted to conduct a workshop. He was 15, so I told him we’d do it," Pinky says.During the summer of 2025, Ayaan began putting together a booklet explaining the central and state government schemes available to domestic workers. He researched the provisions and simplified the information, translating it into Hindi and Marathi so that workers could understand the benefits and registration processes.He also worked on improving his Hindi so he could communicate with participants during the workshops.His mother helped with the arrangements, including approaching housing society committees, organising venues and getting the booklets printed. However, Ayaan took responsibility for explaining the initiative and convincing building managements to host the sessions.Not everyone was immediately receptive. Some housing societies were sceptical, but he continued approaching them.The first workshop was organised in his own apartment complex. It attracted around 80 to 90 domestic workers.Rather than limiting the session to an explanation of government schemes, Ayaan offered practical assistance. He brought his laptop and helped workers navigate the registration portal individually, guiding them through the process.By the end of the workshop, he had registered nearly half the participants. He also collected the contact numbers of those who needed to return to complete their registrations.The exercise marked the beginning of his effort to take the initiative beyond his own residential complex.How 750 workers benefited from the initiativeAs Ayaan began reaching out to more housing societies, the workshops gradually expanded. His initiative has since conducted five workshops and helped more than 750 unorganised-sector workers register for government welfare schemes across Mumbai.One of the beneficiaries is 32-year-old Manisha Dhekde, who has worked as a domestic worker for nearly a decade.She learnt about one of Ayaan's camps through word of mouth and decided to attend. There, she received assistance with obtaining her e-Shram card and enrolling in a post office savings scheme.For her, the experience was an introduction to benefits she had previously known little about."Earlier, I had no idea what an e-Shram card even was," she says."The camp taught me everything patiently."Manisha also says that government benefits have reached her household multiple times since her enrolment. Her experience reflects the practical gap Ayaan is attempting to address: workers may be eligible for government provisions, but without information and assistance with registration, accessing them can remain difficult.Taking the initiative beyond registrationAyaan's work is also rooted in the larger challenges faced by India's unorganised workforce. According to the 2024 India Employment Report, more than 90 per cent of India's workforce is employed in the unorganised sector.Although the e-Shram portal has registered hundreds of millions of workers nationally, many domestic workers continue to face difficulties accessing welfare provisions.Ayaan's initiative, Workers of India, seeks to bridge this gap by taking information and registration assistance directly to workers in residential communities.However, he is now looking at another way to make employment-related information more accessible.Alongside his International Baccalaureate coursework and university applications, the teenager has been developing an AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot. The proposed tool is designed to help domestic workers create bilingual employment contracts without having to navigate complicated forms or online portals.The idea is to allow a worker to describe her employment terms through a voice message in Hindi, Marathi or English. The chatbot would then generate an employment contract in two languages that she could share with her employer.The approach is intended to make the process simpler for workers who may not be comfortable with digital forms or formal documentation.An international recognition for the initiativeAyaan's efforts have also received recognition beyond the housing societies where he conducts his workshops. In July 2026, his initiative, Workers of India, was selected for the International Baccalaureate Global Youth Action Fund.For a teenager balancing schoolwork, university applications and a social initiative, the recognition marks an important milestone.Yet, the problem that first prompted him to act remains.Domestic workers continue to be an essential part of everyday urban life, but many remain unaware of the welfare provisions available to them. Ayaan's experience highlights how access to information and hands-on assistance can help bridge the distance between government schemes and their intended beneficiaries.What began with a woman asking for a loan because her mother was ill has grown into an initiative that has reached more than 750 workers.And for Ayaan, the starting point was a question he could not stop thinking about: "If we didn’t give it to her, what would she have done?"You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘This can’t keep happening’: How divorced military spouses get trapped in foreign countries
articles.summary: Christina Fuller is an American former military spouse living without legal residency in southern Spain, where a custody fight has kept her and her son for y...
articles.body:
Christina Fuller is an American former military spouse living without legal residency in southern Spain, where a custody fight has kept her and her son for years. When her family arrived near the Strait of Gibraltar on US military orders, her son was two. Now, he's nearly 10.

Fuller's marriage to a US Navy sailor assigned to a guided-missile destroyer at Naval Station Rota fell apart soon after the family arrived in 2019.

When her husband filed for divorce in 2021, a Spanish court barred either parent from taking their child out of the country without the other's permission. The next year, the Navy ordered her husband back to the US as the divorce was finalized and Fuller appealed a Spanish custody order.

She eventually won full physical custody and rights similar to legal custody in the US, but she still had to get permission from a judge or her now ex-husband to move their son. By then her son's American passport had also expired, leaving them stuck in Spain.

Fuller says she supports her family by scrapping together an income from this odd job and that – she's a "buscavida," she says, what the Spanish call a hustler.

"I never came to Spain intending to make it my permanent home," Fuller told CNN. "I don't want to feel like a prisoner in another country any more simply because I followed military orders overseas."

When a marriage falls apart, military spouses living overseas can find themselves stranded in foreign countries and bound by foreign custody judgments in their courts — even when those involved are American citizens who moved abroad on US orders. Spouses already made financially vulnerable by years of relocations can be left navigating unfamiliar courts, hiring lawyers in two countries and fighting simply to bring their children home.

Spouses caught in foreign courts have been largely invisible to almost everyone in military circles, including each other. But in August the issue burst into public view when the wife of a Marine Corps officer went viral with an online plea, warning that she and her children could be trapped indefinitely in Germany.

Jamie Lenio said her marriage was ending partly because her husband had an affair with a superior officer, a one-star general — a claim substantiated by a US Africa Command inspector general report obtained by CNN.

Within 48 hours, the video had drawn nearly 500,000 views, more than 30,000 likes and 2,300 comments.

Spouses facing similar circumstances contacted Lenio, leading to an informal network of women, and at least one man, who shared their stories, including on social media, in the hope they, too, can get some help.

Soon after, the military ordered Lenio's husband to return to the US, paving the way for Lenio and her kids to return as well, before a German court could take up the family's case. Earlier this month, Lenio arrived in Southern California with her children.

CNN spoke to more than a dozen current or former spouses of active-duty service members, Defense Department employees or US government contractors who said they were living overseas against their wishes with their children — or had returned to the United States without them — after their marriages ended. All but one of the spouses CNN spoke to were women.

They all described debilitating financial hardship as they fought their legal battles overseas. Many racked up heavy debt, ruined their credit or relied on food banks just to feed their children. Multiple spouses said they skipped meals to get by.

"It's heartbreaking, but it's unfortunately the reality," said Gilbert "Joey" Comley, a retired Army judge advocate who has represented service members and veterans in custody cases involving foreign courts. "Someone always has to have jurisdiction over child custody."

Once a child becomes integrated into daily life abroad, courts may treat that country as the child's "habitual residence" under the 1980 Hague Convention on international child abduction and the US law implementing it.

Legally, that can outweigh citizenship or the fact that the family moved only because of military employment, Comley said.

CNN spoke to military spouses based in Germany, Spain, the UK and Japan, all of whom expressed surprise at having an obscure, international treaty play a role in child custody during and after a divorce. Some said they were blindsided by the power of the foreign court — no matter the country they were in. And they all described incorrect or conflicting guidance from US military officials.

Ahead of deployments or overseas tours, military families often contemplate potential life-changing events, including the death of a service member or illness of a spouse in a structured Family Contingency Plan.

A number of spouses said they wished the military had armed their families with more information so they could incorporate an agreement on how they would approach custody in the event of a divorce overseas.

In response to questions for this story, individual service branches initially directed CNN to the Pentagon for information about the guidance families receive from the military when navigating divorce and child custody in foreign courts. A Pentagon spokesperson then directed CNN back to the individual service branches before highlighting a series of webpages on Military OneSource, a DOD-funded website for military personnel and families. None of the links provide direct support for navigating divorce or child custody in foreign legal systems, a reflection of the dearth of official information available to families before they may be educating themselves in the middle of a crisis.

The Air Force flagged an article that mentioned military divorce overseas, but only that it "can be more complicated than if the couple filed within a state. A US court may not recognize a divorce filed overseas, so it's best to file in the United States." It briefly addressed physical property but not child custody.

The Navy, like other service branches, said it doesn't track how many families are in divorce or child custody proceedings in foreign courts but that it does give them briefings before they go overseas to "ensure service members and their dependents clearly understand host-nation jurisdiction, legal protections, and administrative responsibilities while serving abroad."

Spokespeople for the Marine Corps and the Air Force outlined a number of resources available to military families, including legal-assistance services but with a significant caveat: they would need a private local lawyer to represent them in court.

Across the cases CNN reviewed, a common pattern emerged: The higher-earning partner had an incentive to remain overseas — whether as a service member nearing retirement and eyeing a military contracting job, or as a civilian employee or contractor able to extend an at times lucrative posting long after the marriage ended. Those employment opportunities provide legal status to work in host countries.

The accompanying spouses who were stranded abroad — or felt forced to leave without their children — uniformly described custody proceedings that favored the higher-earning partner, who could afford stronger legal representation and argue that a steadier income left them better positioned to provide for the children.

"It gets expensive," Comley explained, because finding a fair resolution requires retaining a lawyer in the US and another in the foreign country.

For many military spouses, financial independence is elusive , even more so overseas where their job opportunities are further limited by visa restrictions on where they can work. Moving every two to three years makes finding a job or maintaining a career difficult as they contort their lives around their spouse's military service demands.

Though half of active-duty spouses have attained at least a bachelor's degree, the military spouse unemployment rate is about four times higher and they have a median income 42% lower than civilian spouses, according to an analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data by D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families at Syracuse University.

Overseas, employment obstacles multiply as a spouse's legal status extends through their military-connected partner. Once they lose that protection, they have to find an alternate justification for remaining and working in the country while they fight for custodial rights, a costly endeavor.

Military spouses divorcing in foreign courts can also lose out on a major marital asset: US military retirement benefits. Foreign courts may decide divorce and custody but generally do not have jurisdiction to divide those benefits as a US court can, leaving spouses little recourse if the service member refuses to share them voluntarily.

The legal fight often unfolds as an accompanying spouse loses practical support that made overseas life possible: base entry access to affordable shopping, post-office boxes and access to bank accounts or cars tied to the sponsoring spouse. Several CNN spoke with accrued significant credit card debt; one documented relying on a food bank and military-provided thrift-store vouchers.

Jose 'Trey' Gonzalez's marriage deteriorated in 2023, soon after his family moved to Germany for his wife's work with a Defense Department contractor. While a German court considered custody of their now-5-year-old son, Gonzalez's immigration status linked to his wife expired and he left Germany. He saw his son briefly during a 2024 court hearing and visit in Stuttgart but says he has not seen him since.

"I felt like there had to be some kind of workaround because we're all American," Gonzalez told CNN from Florida.

"It's been terrible. It's been a nightmare every day. As long as the Germans have jurisdiction I have zero hope."

In England, Air Force spouse Brandylyn Cohea is torn between staying or going in the wake of her husband filing for a divorce in the United Kingdom.

She fears being deported without her teenage son if she loses her status to work and live in the country. Meanwhile, she worries a court could rule unfavorably if she leaves. The Air Force briefly authorized her and her son to return to the US but they would have had to leave without their two beloved golden retrievers, who came from the US.

She's working up to 55 hours a week while parenting alone, she says, receiving $1300 in child and spousal support per month.

"It's really difficult to watch" other families leave, she says, choking up, "because I want to go home."

Since Lenio's story gained national attention, military spouses facing divorce have increasingly seen public pressure as the only way to force action.

A number have taken their stories public, some appearing in social media videos. Lenio's viral plea in August quickly reached the highest levels of the Navy Department.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who oversees the Marine Corps and was recently nominated to permanently fill the role by President Donald Trump, responded publicly: "We hear you loud and clear. You and your family will be home soon."

The next month, around the time of Cao's nomination, the Marine Corps issued Lenio's husband new orders, and she returned to the US with her children.

Lenio told CNN the video got her home. The Marine Corps said the move was underway before she went public, telling CNN it had already concluded the situation "would be best resolved in the US."

But in short order, the Marine Corps and Navy made similar determinations in the cases of other families.

Several sources – spouses, service members and former military officials familiar with personnel decisions – said Lenio's video was a clear catalyst.

During CNN's reporting, another Marine Corps family facing divorce in Germany also received orders allowing them to return to the US after CNN asked the Pentagon about their situation.

Corina Acevedo, mother of four and the wife of a senior enlisted Marine, said her case began moving only after Lenio's video. Earlier, a German court denied her the authority necessary to return to the US with her children. The Marine Corps would not discuss her case, but said every family's circumstances and timeline are different.

Foreign family court orders can also trump certain decisions by the US military.

Ashlee Gamble's marriage to a Navy sailor fell apart in the summer of 2025 while the couple were living near Kaiserslautern, Germany with their two children. A German court spelled out a custody arrangement after Gamble filed, ultimately unsuccessfully, for the right to determine where her children would reside.

"You're sucked into the German court system. And all of it is in German," she said.

Last year, over her husband's objections, the military granted a request for Gamble to return to the US with both children, but the German court would allow her to leave only with her eldest child. Her young son would remain in Germany with her husband.

Stars and Stripes first reported on the family earlier this month. Two days later, Gamble's Navy-appointed legal advisor let her know the Navy had released orders to move her husband and family back to the US, more than a year after a military-provided clinical social worker first recommended Gamble return with the two children.

Gamble's husband says the orders have upended his family's lives in the middle of his children's school year, and he questioned why the Navy would intervene in a private family matter.

"I think that civil matters should be handled by the civil courts and not have the military involved," he told CNN, outlining what he sees as advantages for military spouses in the German court system.

"It's going to cost them more in the US because here in Germany, if they can't get a job, they're provided access to a free lawyer for a civil case. Where in the US are you going to get a free divorce lawyer?"

But Gamble says her court-appointed lawyer is managing many cases besides hers and she is relieved to be leaving Germany and heading back to the US.

"I feel like military families have no business being in German courts unless someone broke a law. But when it comes to custody, this can't keep happening."

Even so, the German court order will cross the Atlantic with the family, dictating their custody arrangement unless or until the German court relinquishes jurisdiction.

Without a treaty change or a Pentagon-wide policy, commands and contractors retain broad discretion over whether a family can return home to pursue divorce and custody in an American court. Families described officials who were ill-informed or unwilling to intervene and others who were supportive and responsive but still unable to force a resolution once a foreign court became involved.

Efforts to bring attention to this specific issue have coincided with a broad new policy focus on military family struggles amid the Iran War and the early days of Trump's Military Spouse Commission, a panel led by Jennifer Hegseth, wife of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The commission's membership includes almost all of the spouses of the military's top brass. The commission is tasked with, among other things, developing "policy recommendations to address … deployment-related support" and "improve the quality of life for military spouses while supporting the highest standard of military readiness," according to the White House.

Christina Fuller watched military interventions for other families from Spain.

"When I saw Jamie's story come out and I saw the Secretary of the Navy saying 'not on my watch,' I thought, 'OK, sir, let's see what's going to happen on your watch,' because this has been happening for a long time," she said.

Her ex-husband returned to Spain on military orders last year, she says, and now has brief regular visits and calls with their son.

However, Fuller is no longer a military dependent, limiting the Navy's ability to resolve her case through new orders or an early return program. Her son remains a military dependent, though Fuller says he was unable to receive on-base health care for the years his father was in Hawaii.

An email Fuller provided from the naval hospital in Rota showed records incorrectly identifying the child as living in Hawaii with his father, who told CNN he included his son on his military orders.

He said it has been "extremely difficult" being separated from his son and "navigating different legal systems and military obligations presents significant challenges."

Fuller has sought help from three congressional offices and the US consulate, but says she has been unable to obtain a US passport for her son without his father's consent.

While she still wants to return to the US, for now she is building a life for her children: play dates, basketball practice, dance classes and birthday parties. Her son now has an American half-brother, and Fuller has learned Spanish while studying European law and the Hague Convention as she works to provide other families information on social media.

"Even if it's too late to give me those years back, it is not too late to make sure somebody else doesn't lose theirs."

articles.title: Woman Goes to Victoria’s Secret With Her Husband for a Return. Then the Cashier Asks About ‘Other Items’ She Had Never Seen
articles.summary: A Victoria's Secret return took a surprising turn when a cashier asked about other items the customer had never seen.
articles.body:
A routine return at Victoria's Secret reportedly took an unexpected turn when a cashier asked a customer whether she also wanted to return other items she had never seen before.

The moment was shared on Instagram by a creator who goes by Astra, who was waiting in line behind the woman. According to Astra, the customer was returning a gift her husband had bought for her, and he was standing with her at the counter.

The exchange has since drawn attention online, with commenters weighing in on what the cashier meant.

Astra said she was waiting her turn when the woman in front of her reached the register.

In her first post, Astra told viewers the woman was returning something her husband had picked out. She joked that he had apparently relied on guesswork. She also claimed that the cashier asked whether the woman wanted to return the other items purchased on the account.

According to Astra, the woman then asked the cashier which items she was referring to. The cashier then reportedly listed lace bodysuits and matching sets that the customer had apparently never seen before. She described them as honeymoon-level purchases and noted they did not appear to be in the woman's size.

Astra questioned in her video why the cashier would start listing such items at the register. The creator said, "I had never in my life wanted to mind my business less." She described the moment as the first piece of evidence in an investigation into the husband.

The husband allegedly tried to explain away the purchases, claiming they must have been a mistake. He suggested that his mother might have accidentally used their rewards account. According to Astra, the wife checked her phone as her husband stuttered before calmly pointing out that the purchases coincided with his Thursday golf league.

The cashier then reportedly said she remembered him because he never let his girlfriend use store coupons.

Astra took the comment to mean the extra purchases were meant for the husband's girlfriend. She joked that the girlfriend seemingly received the premium gifts while the wife got far less.

Many commenters believed the cashier shared the information on purpose. One user wrote, "The employee knew what the husband was doing and used the return as her way of helping the wife."

Another said, "Immediately clocked her as a girl's girl trying to help! Cashiers don't ask that." One also noted the wife's behavior and said, "Screaming is normal, but when they stay calm you know it's gonna be scary."

Several users who identified themselves as Victoria's Secret employees claimed similar situations happen often. Others praised the cashier, with one joking that some heroes wear Victoria's Secret wings.

articles.title: Meet Bhavitha Mandava, the Hyderabad-born architecture student who was discovered at a New York subway station, rose to the Chanel runway and has now earned Instagram recognition
articles.summary: A chance encounter on a New York subway platform changed the course of Bhavitha Mandava’s life.
articles.body: A chance encounter on a New York subway platform changed the course of Bhavitha Mandava’s life. At the time, she was a student with no professional modelling experience. Today, the Hyderabad-born model has walked for some of the biggest names in international fashion, opened a Chanel runway show and become a Chanel House Ambassador. Now, she has another achievement to add to her growing list: being named one of the 25 global winners of Instagram’s Rings Award 2026.The 26-year-old model has attracted attention not only for her runway appearances but also for the unusual path that brought her into the fashion industry. Her journey began far from fashion studios and modelling agencies, with an encounter that eventually introduced her to the world of luxury fashion.A subway encounter that changed everythingBorn into a Telugu family in Andhra Pradesh and raised in Hyderabad, Bhavitha did not initially set out to become a model. She studied architecture at Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University before moving to New York to pursue a Master of Science in Integrated Design and Media, with a focus on human-computer interaction. Her life took an unexpected turn in September 2024 when Matthieu Blazy, who was then the creative director of Bottega Veneta, noticed her at a New York subway station. She was wearing jeans and a T-shirt and had no previous modelling experience.Recalling the experience in an interview with Coveteur, Bhavitha said she had been scouted at the subway station just a week before meeting Blazy. She also spoke about how quickly he believed in her potential. “I had been scouted in a subway station just a week before meeting him. I had no prior experience, but the moment I met Matthieu, he believed in me completely,” she told the publication. The opportunity soon turned into a professional debut. Bhavitha walked as an exclusive model for Bottega Veneta's Spring/Summer 2025 show in Milan and also appeared in the brand's campaign. What began as an unexpected discovery had opened the door to an international modelling career.From Bottega Veneta to making history at ChanelBhavitha's association with Blazy continued to bring her into the spotlight. When he moved to Chanel, she went on to achieve another significant milestone in her career. In December 2025, she opened Chanel's Métiers d'Art 2026 show, becoming the first Indian model to open a Chanel runway presentation. The achievement brought her wider recognition in the fashion industry and marked an important moment for Indian representation on an international luxury runway.The setting also added an interesting connection to her story. The Chanel show was presented in a New York subway station, bringing her journey full circle from the place where she had first been noticed. In March 2026, Bhavitha reached another milestone when she became the first Indian model to be named a Chanel House Ambassador. She has also appeared on the covers of international fashion publications, including British Vogue and Numéro France.Her background in architecture and design remains part of her identity. Rather than presenting only polished fashion images, she also shares glimpses of the creative process, backstage moments and the people behind the industry.Why Instagram recognised Bhavitha MandavaInstagram has named Bhavitha among the 25 winners of its Rings Award for 2026. The annual recognition programme was launched in October 2025 to celebrate creators who bring originality, creativity and a distinctive perspective to the platform. The award is not intended to be based simply on follower numbers. Instead, it recognises people whose work makes an impact through creative expression and their willingness to explore different ideas. Bhavitha has around 7.4 lakh followers on Instagram. In its announcement, Instagram highlighted how she moved from being a student in New York to becoming a recognised face in international fashion.The platform described her discovery by Blazy, her debut as a Bottega Veneta exclusive, her achievement at Chanel and her appointment as a House Ambassador. It also drew attention to the way she shares her experience of the fashion world, combining backstage glimpses with her design sensibility. Bhavitha is among the Indian names recognised in this year's awards. Kerala-based freestyle footballer Muhammed Riswan has also been named a winner. Together, their inclusion reflects the range of creative work being recognised by the platform, from fashion and design to sport.A marble ring and a new kind of Instagram recognitionThe 25 winners will receive more than a digital announcement. Each will be presented with a physical ring featuring a four-leaf clover carved from Connemara marble, a distinctive green stone from Ireland. The winners will also receive special digital benefits on Instagram, including the option to customise the background colour of their profiles. These features give the recognition a visible presence on the platform.For Bhavitha, the award marks another chapter in a career that has taken an unexpected route. She moved from studying architecture in India to pursuing higher education in New York, where a chance encounter introduced her to modelling. Within a short period, she went on to work with Bottega Veneta, make history at Chanel and become a House Ambassador.Her latest recognition celebrates not just her presence on international runways but also the creative perspective she brings to the digital space. From a subway platform to one of the world's most recognised fashion houses, Bhavitha's journey shows how an unexpected opportunity can open doors to an entirely new career.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nick Lacy breaks silence on ‘$12,000’ Japan restaurant bill after viewers flood table with food orders
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has addressed the backlash over his claims that he paid $12,000 at a restaurant in Japan after viewers allegedly placed food
articles.body: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has addressed the backlash over his claims that he paid $12,000 at a restaurant in Japan after viewers allegedly placed food orders using his table’s QR code. The 23-year-old admitted that he was joking about paying the entire amount and later realised he had misunderstood the situation. In a post on X on October 29, 2026, Lacy explained that a language barrier caused the confusion. He also apologised to the restaurant for not correcting his earlier statements sooner.Nick “Lacy” explains why he joked about paying $12,000 at a restaurant in JapanThe controversy started during Lacy's October 28 livestream from Japan. While eating at a restaurant, the streamer reportedly showed the QR code used by customers to place food orders. Some viewers noticed it and allegedly started ordering food for his table without his permission.Things became uncomfortable when restaurant staff approached him about the additional orders. Lacy initially said that the total had reached around 1.6 million Japanese yen, which he described as almost $12,000.During the livestream, he expressed his frustration with viewers and complained about the amount of food they had ordered. He also said he had offered to pay for the extra food and asked the restaurant to give it to other families rather than waste it.However, his claims soon faced questions on Reddit. Several users on the r/LivestreamFail subreddit accused him of making the story sound worse than it actually was.One Reddit user, Apart-Volume9340, claimed that restaurant staff had asked Lacy several times whether the additional orders belonged to him. According to the user, the staff never prepared most of the food and instead gave him a receipt so he could identify the items he had actually ordered.Another user, valcatrina, also questioned the $12,000 claim and argued that the restaurant would not simply charge him for food ordered by strangers.The restaurant's side of the story also became part of the discussion. According to a report by Dexerto on October 29, Zauo Shibuya denied charging customers for food they had not ordered. Its reported statement said staff checked orders with customers and only charged them for items they had consumed. The restaurant also acknowledged that some extra dishes had already been prepared.Nick “Lacy” apologises to the restaurant and admits he made a mistakeFollowing the criticism, Lacy shared a detailed explanation on X on October 29. He said he initially believed he was responsible for the entire amount because of the language barrier.According to the streamer, he had agreed to cover the bill and left his assistant to handle the situation after his livestream was interrupted. He later returned to streaming while still believing he owed $12,000. This was when he started joking about the situation.He wrote:"I wanna clear up the restaurant situation in Japan. Due to the language barrier, I genuinely thought I was responsible for a $12,000 bill initially. I told the restaurant I’d cover it, asked them to give the extra food to families, and left my assistant to handle everything because my stream was cut and i wanted to get back."Lacy then admitted that he continued making jokes without knowing the complete situation. He also explained that he only learned later that he had to pay for the additional food that had already been prepared, rather than the entire amount.The streamer accepted that his failure to correct the story earlier was his mistake."Where I went wrong was not correcting the story once I found out. I never expected it to go so viral, and im dumb and thought it was funny."Lacy further said that he was not bothered by the criticism itself, but he did care about the attention the restaurant received because of his comments.He added that he had contacted the restaurant to make things right and apologised for not explaining the situation sooner. He also made it clear that the restaurant was not responsible for what happened.Importantly, Lacy has not revealed the exact amount he eventually paid for the additional food. His clarification makes it clear that the $12,000 figure was what he initially believed he owed, not the confirmed amount he paid.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independence
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The successful night launch of Isro’s navigation satellite NVS-03 carrying an indigenously-manufactured atomic clock along with procured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The successful night launch of Isro’s navigation satellite NVS-03 carrying an indigenously-manufactured atomic clock along with procured (foreign) atomic clocks on Friday will make India’s indigenous satellite navigation system NaVIC or desi GPS up and running again. The success of GSLV-F18 mission is a big boost for India’s strategic forces as they are till now dependent on foreign navigation systems like American GPS and Russian GLONASS for missile navigation.NaVIC was down to three active satellites as compared to the minimum quorum of four needed to keep the navigation system operational. But as four operational satellites are required for a standalone GPS-style position tracking system to work, NaVIC is currently not being used by the armed forces for the purposes of missile navigation, precise positioning and coordination of warships at sea, and indigenous navigation support for troop movement and combat aircraft. The strategic forces are, therefore, dependent on foreign navigation systems like American GPS and Russian GLONASS.Relying on foreign-operated navigation systems like GPS creates a critical dependency under which access can be restricted, downgraded or completely cut off during a conflict or a war, as India had experienced during the 1999 Kargil war.But the successful launch of NVS-03 has changed everything. It will make the NavIC constellation not only operational for strategic use but also for civilian use across India and up to 1,500 km (930 miles) beyond the country's geographical borders.After the successful launch, space minister Jitendra Singh posted on X on Friday night, “Congratulations Team Isro for the successful launch of GSLV-F18/NVS-03 mission! This remarkable achievement reflects India's growing prowess in Space technology and our unwavering commitment to strengthening sovereign indigenous navigation capabilities. With revolutionary Space reforms announced by PM Shri Narendra Modi ji in recent years, India's success stories in Space vindicate the dream of founding fathers Vikram Sarabhai and Satish Dhawan. Today is the celebration of another proud moment for India!”Indian security forces need an operational NavIC to maintain strategic autonomy and secure tactical advantage without relying on foreign-controlled networks. The four-satellite constellation will ensure secure, uncompromised communication, mobility and targeting data. Modern military hardware such as ballistic missiles and precision-guided munitions require highly accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals to function effectively.NavIC was originally designed with a constellation of seven satellites and a network of ground stations operating 24 x 7. Three satellites of the constellation were placed in geostationary orbit, at 32.5°E, 83°E and 129.5°E respectively, and four satellites in inclined geosynchronous orbit with equatorial crossing of 55°E and 111.75°E respectively, with inclination of 29° (two satellites in each plane). But with time, NavIC came down to three satellites as replacement satellites could not be placed in orbit due to setbacks. NVS-02 satellite was launched on Jan 29, 2025, but it failed to reach the intended orbit due to a pyro valve signal loss in the engine.

articles.title: In 2018, a solo hiker walked nearly 8,000 miles across America’s biggest trails in 251 days after already logging over 40,000 miles on foot
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Heather Anderson, the first woman to hike the Appalachian, Pacific Crest, and Continental Divide Trails, and her record-breaking 8,000-mile trek in 251 days.
articles.body: A trekker by the name of Heather Anderson became the first woman to complete the Triple Crown of Hiking three times across the Appalachian Trail, Pacific Crest Trail, and Continental Divide Trail. The achievement was set in stone on 8 November, 2018 after she completed the final section of the Continental Divide Trail in New Mexico. According to National Geographic, during the 2018 challenge, Anderson covered 7,944 miles and finished the hike in 251 days, 20 hours, and 10 minutes, for which she was named the 2019 Adventurer of the Year. Later, the California Outdoors Hall of Fame reported that she had logged more than 40,000 foot-miles, up from 28,000, since beginning her hiking career in 2003.Three trails accomplished in a single year and other recordsIn the world of hiking, there’s a coveted honour called the Triple Crown, which is only earned by people who have completed the Appalachian Trail, Pacific Crest Trail, and Continental Divide Trail. Anderson had completed each trail three times, and in doing so became one of the few women to achieve that feat. Her historic journey began in the year 2018, when her schedule lined all three routes into one year. It started off with her completion of both the Appalachian Trail and the Pacific Crest Trail earlier in the year, leaving only the Continental Divide Trail to conquer as winter approached in November.Triumphing over the three routes was no small feat since it required hikers to cover long distances on foot across varied terrain in different regions of the United States. However, Anderson wasn’t a stranger to pushing limits; her own monumental achievement was preceded by earlier records on individual trails. In 2013, it took her only 60 days, 17 hours, and 12 minutes to cover the Pacific Crest Trail, which extended over 2,655 miles, the California Outdoors Hall of Fame noted.She continued to stack up new records in 2015; Anderson completed the Appalachian Trail, a route that runs from Georgia to Mount Katahdin in Maine, in 54 days, seven hours, and 48 minutes. On top of that, in the following year, she covered the 800-mile Arizona Trail in 19 days, 17 hours, and nine minutes, setting yet another women's speed record.From college graduate to a historic hikerAnderson’s path to hiking started while she was working at the Grand Canyon, and after she had graduated from Anderson University in 2003, she decided to attempt the Appalachian Trail. Prior to that, she had not considered herself to be an athletic person, while adopting the trail name Anish in honour of the Anishinabe heritage of her great-great-grandmother. Her university’s alumni profile shows Anderson’s ambition in her younger days was to be ordained and work as a missionary abroad. Moreover, her career as a hiker didn’t particularly follow the trajectory of a straight line; she fell back to ordinary life, taking up conventional employment in Seattle, married but eventually left the job and divorced before pursuing her passion for long-distance hiking. Anderson's account of why she continued returning to the outdoors was explained to National Geographic: “I feel like there are things greater than us, and I feel a connection to that when I am in the outdoors. Anytime I’m in nature, [that connection is] everywhere around me.”Subsequently, she went on to become an author and professional speaker and published Thirst: 2,600 Miles to Home in 2019 and Mud, Rocks, Blazes: Letting Go on the Appalachian Trail in 2021. Her other literary work includes co-authoring with Katie Gerber the book titled Adventure Ready: A Hiker’s Guide to Training, Planning, and Resiliency in 2022.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1974, more than 6,000 peregrine falcons were released into the wild after the population wiped out; helping restore the once-endangered birds across North America
articles.summary: In the early 1974s, American peregrine falcons were struggling to survive in parts of North America.
articles.body: In the early 1974s, American peregrine falcons were struggling to survive in parts of North America. Years of DDT use had left many eggs with thin shells that could crack during incubation, leaving fewer chicks to hatch. Conservationists responded by breeding the birds in captivity and releasing them into the wild. According to the National Park Service (NPS), more than 6,000 American peregrines were released through recovery programmes. Restrictions on DDT and legal protection also played a part in the comeback. Along Alaska’s rivers, long-term surveys later recorded a rise in nesting pairs. The American peregrine falcon was removed from the US federal endangered and threatened species list in 1999.Peregrine falcon subspecies faced different levels of pesticide riskThe decline of peregrine falcons was closely associated with the use of DDT, an insecticide that became widespread during the mid-20th century. As the chemical passed through food chains, residues accumulated in birds of prey. Its breakdown product, DDE, interfered with eggshell formation, leaving eggs too fragile to withstand the weight of an incubating adult. Fewer chicks survived to hatch, putting pressure on populations that were already struggling.By 1970, the American and Arctic subspecies of peregrine falcon had been listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1969. Peale's peregrines, found along parts of the Pacific coast, were not listed because their breeding populations had remained comparatively stable and exposure to DDT was limited.Restrictions on DDT changed the course of recoveryThe United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) banned DDT for most uses in the country in 1972, using powers granted under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act. The restriction followed growing evidence of the damage the chemical was causing to wildlife, particularly birds whose survival depended on successful breeding.The change did not remove every source of exposure. DDE residues continued to be detected in some areas, while peregrines travelling to wintering grounds in Latin America could encounter pesticides that remained in use there. Even so, reducing DDT use in the United States helped create better conditions for the birds to reproduce.Legal protection and pesticide restrictions were accompanied by a coordinated recovery programme. The US Fish and Wildlife Service brought together federal and state agencies, independent biologists and conservation organisations to identify measures that could restore declining populations.Captive-bred birds helped rebuild depleted populationsScientists at Cornell University developed successful methods for breeding and raising peregrine falcons in captivity. The young birds could then be introduced into suitable habitats through a technique known as hacking, which gives them time to adjust to their surroundings before becoming independent.For the releases, young falcons were placed in specially designed boxes positioned on towers or cliff ledges. Food was supplied through a chute during the early stages, limiting the birds' contact with people. Once they were old enough, the boxes were opened and the young falcons could begin exploring the area and exercising their wings.Food was gradually reduced as the birds developed their flying and hunting abilities. The intention was to give them a chance to establish themselves in the wild rather than remain dependent on human care.The programme involved the US Fish and Wildlife Service, state wildlife agencies, The Peregrine Fund, the Santa Cruz Predatory Bird Research Group and the Midwestern Peregrine Falcon Restoration Project. Together, these efforts resulted in the release of more than 6,000 American peregrines from 1974 onwards.Arctic peregrines recovered without captive releasesThe Arctic peregrine population had fallen by as much as 80%, but enough birds survived that captive-bred releases were not considered necessary for its recovery.Restrictions on DDT and protection under the Endangered Species Act helped numbers increase. In 1984, the Arctic subspecies was moved from endangered to threatened status, reflecting an improvement in its prospects. A decade later, in October 1994, the US Fish and Wildlife Service announced that the population had recovered sufficiently for the subspecies to be removed from the federal list of threatened and endangered species.Thousands of Arctic peregrines now occur across North America. Their recovery also demonstrated that populations could rebound when the pressures responsible for their decline were reduced, even without the extensive release programmes used for American peregrines.Surveys along Alaska's rivers track the returnIn Alaska's Yukon-Charley Rivers National Preserve, biologists have monitored peregrine falcons since the mid-1970s. During an early survey in 1975, they recorded 11 nesting pairs. More recent surveys in comparable areas have documented more than 50 to 60 pairs, providing a long-term indication of how the population has changed.The work involves searching cliffs and bluffs where peregrines establish nests, observing birds and recording their breeding activity. The terrain can make surveys demanding, but repeated visits allow scientists to compare nesting activity across years and assess whether birds continue to occupy established territories.The American peregrine falcon was removed from the federal endangered and threatened species list in August 1999. The decision followed a substantial recovery attributed to pesticide restrictions, legal protection and the release of captive-bred birds.Monitoring continued after federal protection endedDelisting did not mean that monitoring stopped. The US Fish and Wildlife Service established a schedule of post-delisting checks to determine whether populations remained stable after federal protection was withdrawn. Surveys were carried out in 2003, with further monitoring planned for 2006, 2009, 2012 and 2015.Results from the 2003 assessment estimated about 3,000 breeding pairs across the United States, Canada and Mexico. Researchers also examined territory occupancy, nesting success and productivity, measures that help show whether birds are reproducing successfully rather than simply appearing in greater numbers.You use AI every day. articles.title: 1930s: Eva Howie made her daughter Barbara a dollhouse with bread dough furnishings; her family preserved it for decades before donating it to a museum
articles.summary: Discover the captivating story of Eva Howie's handcrafted dollhouse from the 1930s, complete with unique bread-dough furnishings, and learn how it became a cherished family heirloom before being donated to the National Museum of Australia.
articles.body: In the 1930s, Eva Howie of Eden Hills, South Australia, made a dollhouse for her daughter, Barbara Hetherington. Alongside purchased furniture, Howie crafted tiny furnishings from bread dough, creating a detailed miniature home that the family carefully preserved for decades. Eva Howie made the dollhouse for her eldest daughter, Barbara Hetherington, in the 1930s, furnishing it with tiny objects, some handcrafted from bread dough. The family treasured the house and kept it in excellent condition for more than 50 years before donating it to the National Museum of Australia in 1991. The details of its construction and preservation reflect the family’s care and Howie’s craftsmanship. The museum’s collection history of the Hetherington dollhouse documents its maker, furnishings and preservation.A mother’s gift from a favourite bookEva Howie (1880-1972) lived in Eden Hills, SA. The house was based on an illustration from Millicent Mouse and Her Funny Wee House, a children’s book that had been a favourite of her daughter Barbara’s youth. Booksellers catalogue the book as ‘A Story in Easy Rhyme’ by Arthur Mansbridge, illustrated by Jessie May Ellerby and published by Frederick Warne in 1927.Barbara Hetherington, who was born in 1911, was an adult when she received the dollhouse. The gift was inspired by a book she had loved as a child, making it a personal keepsake as well as a carefully crafted miniature home. The Hetherington dollhouse was made to be admired rather than used as a plaything. Later generations were not allowed to play with it, helping preserve its furnishings and delicate details. The family’s care kept the miniature house in excellent condition for more than five decades.Inside the houseThe house is a clever piece of design. The roof pops off to reveal an attic, and the walls fall away to disclose two rooms on the ground floor. There is a stairway in the front room and a fireplace in the rear one. The house sits on a dark green garden base, manicured with miniature flowerbeds complete with glass daffodils and fabric tulips.The furnishings combine purchased and handmade pieces, including beds, quilts, crocheted floor mats and handwritten newspapers. Many of the smallest objects were crafted from bread dough, showcasing Howie’s attention to detail. Archival photographs from the National Museum of Australia document conservator Cathy Collins carrying out treatment on the dollhouse’s exterior, highlighting the specialist work required to preserve a fragile object of this kind.Why it survivedThe removable roof reveals an attic, while sliding walls expose the two ground-floor rooms. Because the dollhouse was treated as a display piece, later generations were not allowed to play with it. That care helped preserve its delicate structure and furnishings until the family donated it to the museum in 1991.The dollhouse is now part of the National Museum of Australia’s National Historical Collection, which includes hundreds of toys and objects associated with childhood. It was included in the museum’s Play display, held from 26 June 2021 to 14 February 2022. The Hetherington dollhouse brings together a family story, a childhood book and Howie’s detailed craftsmanship. Made in the 1930s and preserved by the family for decades, it remains part of the National Museum of Australia’s collection. Access to collection objects not on public display requires an appointment, and the museum warns that visits may be affected by its long-term storage project from 2026. Anyone hoping to view the dollhouse should contact the museum in advance through its collection access information page.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1966, an elderly Brooklyn resident launched a tree campaign that brought 1,500 trees back to Bed-Stuy
articles.summary: Discover how Hattie Carthan, an elderly resident of Brooklyn, transformed Bedford Stuyvesant by planting over 1,500 trees, enhancing the neighborhood's beauty and community spirit. Her legacy thrives through landmarks and initiatives that continue to flourish today.
articles.body: Seldom do street trees receive the recognition they merit. They make a row of brownstones feel more like a neighbourhood than a hallway, chill the pavement, and muffle the cacophony of a busy block. No one sends a notification when they pass away. They just thin out, and in the 1960s many blocks in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, lost trees that were never replaced. One resident chose to act. In 1966, Hattie Carthan, then in her mid-sixties and living on Vernon Avenue, helped organise the Bedford-Stuyvesant Beautification Committee. Her campaign connected neighbourhood groups with city officials and turned tree planting into a broader community movement. She later helped protect a historic magnolia and establish an environmental centre.A block that lost its treesCarthan was born in Virginia in 1900, and her family moved to New York in 1928. She settled on Vernon Avenue in 1953, when the block still had a line of street trees. By 1964, only three of the original trees remained. That year, she and seven neighbours formed the T&T Vernon Avenue Block Association after she sent postcards inviting residents to join the effort.Winning support took persistence. Some neighbours worried that leaves would mean more raking and extra rubbish, while others questioned the value of replacing the trees. Carthan argued that trees would improve the street’s appearance and property values. In 1965, the association held a barbecue, selling plates for $1.25 and raising $200, enough to buy four trees. Some neighbours called her a “tree nut,” but the first saplings gave the campaign a visible start.A deal with City HallAt the association’s second barbecue in 1966, Carthan invited Mayor John Lindsay. He agreed to support a tree matching program under which the city would plant six trees for every four planted by residents. The Parks Department announced the partnership in 1967, describing it as a joint effort between community groups and city agencies. The department’s contemporary announcement outlined the plan.The campaign grew beyond one block. The Bedford-Stuyvesant Beautification Committee eventually brought together more than 100 block associations, and the movement planted more than 1,500 trees, including ginkgo, sycamore, honey locust and elm. The historical record of the Hattie Carthan Collection documents the committee’s reach and planting total. In 1967, the city also budgeted $1.2 million for tree planting and care, although the available record does not establish that Carthan’s campaign directly caused the budget decision. The Neighbourhood Tree Corps came later. In 1971, Carthan and her colleagues established the program with a grant from the New York State Council on the Arts. It taught young people how to care for street trees, extending the campaign’s work to a new generation.The magnolia and the Earth CentreThe magnolia on Lafayette Avenue became another focus of Carthan’s work. Planted in 1885, the Southern magnolia faced a threat when redevelopment plans put the neighbouring brownstones at risk. At a public hearing, Carthan argued that saving the tree could also preserve the buildings behind it: “If we save the tree, we save the structures behind it.” She formed the Magnolia Tree Committee, raised money for a protective wall and campaigned for landmark status. The city designated the magnolia a living landmark in 1970. The Brooklyn Botanic Garden’s history of Carthan and the magnolia documents the preservation campaign and the importance of the surrounding buildings.Carthan also worked to secure the three neighbouring brownstones, negotiating the proposed purchase price down from $25,000 to $1,200. The Magnolia Tree Earth Centre was established in 1972 and incorporated as a nonprofit in 1973. Fundraising concerts featuring folk singer Pete Seeger in 1974 and 1977 supported the effort to establish a permanent neighbourhood institution. The buildings later became the center’s headquarters, which opened to the public after renovation in 1979.Carthan also helped establish the Green Guerillas, a group involved in the community garden movement. She died in 1984, but her work continued through neighbourhood planting and environmental education. In 1998, the garden beside the Earth Centre was named in her honour. articles.body: NEW DELHI: World Bank has said that poverty in India, defined at $4.2 a day, will decline from 14.2% in 2026 to 12.1% by 2028.Between 2011 and 2023, it is estimated that the share of the population living below $4.2 a day declined from 57.7% to 16.1%, lifting an estimated 496 million people out of poverty. It said that extreme poverty ($3 a day) declined from 27.1% to 2.6% during this period."This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth; rising employment, especially among women; and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment, and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023," World Bank said in its latest Poverty & Equity brief.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman cheered the decline in poverty in the country, pointing out that the report recognised India's progress as a country with one of the fastest poverty declines in the world."Under the leadership of PM Narendra Modi, govt's sustained policy efforts are yielding tangible results, strengthening the foundations for inclusive growth and greater economic opportunity. This is the reason why NDA govt wins people's trust and mandate of our citizens. We remain committed to building on this progress through productive employment, stronger household incomes and effective delivery of public services, so that aspirations of our people are met," she posted on X.World Bank also noted that between 2017 and 2023, employment increased by about 134 million people, nearly twice the growth of the working-age population, with major gains driven by rural women entering paid work and raising the number of earners in households."Labour market conditions continue to be broadly resilient, with labour force participation and employment rates stable between Q1 FY 2026 and Q1 FY 2027. articles.body: Residents in Washington, DC, were left frightened after a large aircraft flew unusually low over their neighbourhoods on Thursday evening, prompting several people to call 911 fearing that a plane was about to crash. The couple was holding baskets of candy as they watched the plane pass.However, the surprise spectacle left several Washington residents alarmed rather than entertained, Daily Beast reported.One Milen Rodban also said she was caught off guard by the unexpected flyover and had “a mini heart attack along with everyone else on the street.”Even the DC City Council said it was startled by the manoeuvre, criticising the short notice given to people in the area.“This flyover provided just fifteen minutes' notice to anyone in downtown DC, at the Pentagon, or at National Airport,” the council wrote on X. “It startled many, including us.”The Federal Aviation Administration told The Daily Beast that the flyover had been coordinated with the agency. articles.title: Paul Rosolie entered the Amazon at 18 and spent two decades fighting to save its rainforest; now, his team is protecting 160,000 acres of forest
articles.summary: When American naturalist and conservationist Paul Rosolie first travelled to the Peruvian Amazon at 18, he was drawn to one of the world's most
articles.body: When American naturalist and conservationist Paul Rosolie first travelled to the Peruvian Amazon at 18, he was drawn to one of the world's most extraordinary wildernesses. Two decades later, his work has evolved from exploring remote forests and studying wildlife into a long-term effort to protect the rainforest from illegal logging, road expansion and other threats. Working alongside Indigenous conservationist Juan Julio Durand and local communities, Rosolie helped establish Junglekeepers, a nonprofit focused on safeguarding the Las Piedras watershed in Peru's Madre de Dios region. The organisation now reports that its rangers safeguard almost 160,000 acres of rainforest. But with illegal activities and drug trafficking threatening the region, the team says its work is far from over.Paul Rosolie's journey from Amazon explorer to conservationistRosolie's connection with the Amazon began when he travelled to Peru as a teenager. Over the years, he explored remote parts of the rainforest, documented wildlife and became increasingly concerned about the destruction of habitats that had remained largely intact.One of the people who helped shape his conservation journey was Juan Julio Durand, a member of the local Indigenous community who was already working in the region. Their partnership grew around the Las Piedras River, a waterway in southeastern Peru that passes through ecologically important rainforest.According to Mongabay, Rosolie and Durand shifted their focus towards protecting the forest as roads and other forms of development began encroaching on the area. Their efforts eventually developed into Junglekeepers, bringing together local conservation work, ranger patrols and fundraising to help safeguard threatened rainforest.Rosolie has described the journey as a long and uncertain one. In a February 2026 interview with Mongabay, he reflected on the personal and financial sacrifices involved, explaining that it took roughly 20 years before he began to see conservation work achieve results on a larger scale.What is Junglekeepers, and how does it protect the Amazon?Junglekeepers works in the Madre de Dios region of Peru, focusing on the Las Piedras watershed, part of the wider Amazon rainforest. The area is known for its rich biodiversity and contains forests that face growing pressure from human activity.The organisation's approach combines land acquisition, local employment and forest monitoring. According to Junglekeepers, it seeks to acquire land in areas threatened by logging and land grabbing, while employing local people as rangers to patrol and monitor the forest.The ranger programme involves more than walking through the rainforest. The organisation says its operating costs include ranger salaries, food and accommodation, boats, fuel, communications equipment, trail maintenance and ranger stations.By employing people with local knowledge, Junglekeepers aims to strengthen conservation efforts while creating livelihoods connected to protecting the forest. Its work also involves monitoring wildlife and responding to threats such as forest fires and illegal activity.How much rainforest is the team protecting?Junglekeepers' reported conservation footprint has grown considerably in recent years. In its annual report announcement published on March 3, 2025, the organisation said it had expanded its protected area from 49,000 acres to 107,000 acres during 2024.Its current mission page reports that its rangers safeguard almost 160,000 acres. The organisation's broader ambition is to protect approximately 300,000 acres across the Las Piedras corridor.Illegal logging and drug trafficking threaten the forestDespite the reported expansion, protecting the rainforest remains difficult. Junglekeepers identifies illegal logging, poaching, gold mining and road development among the threats facing the Las Piedras region.The concern is not limited to trees being cut down. Roads can open previously remote areas to further settlement and extraction, fragment habitats and make it easier for illegal activities to spread into intact forest.In its February 2026 interview with Mongabay, Rosolie also described the growing danger posed by drug traffickers operating in the region. He said the organisation had faced serious threats and was working more closely with Peruvian law enforcement because confronting organised criminal groups required capabilities beyond those of conservation rangers.The risks underline the difference between establishing a conservation area and ensuring that it remains safe over time. Rangers need equipment, transport, reliable funding and support from authorities to monitor remote areas and respond to threats.Junglekeepers' January 2026 announcement of its End Game campaign also referred to escalating violence, including an armed vehicle ambush targeting conservation leaders and local communities. The campaign aimed to secure an additional 50,000 acres considered at risk.Protecting the rainforest also matters for Indigenous communitiesThe Las Piedras region is home to Indigenous communities and includes areas associated with the Mashco Piro, also known as the Nomole, an Indigenous people living in voluntary isolation.Protecting the forest can help preserve the territory and natural resources on which Indigenous communities depend. For peoples living in voluntary isolation, incursions by outsiders can pose particularly serious risks, including exposure to disease, violence and disruption of their way of life.Junglekeepers has said that establishing a buffer zone is part of its effort to protect the Mashco Piro from incursions linked to illegal logging. The organisation's work in this area must be understood alongside the need to respect Indigenous peoples' rights, autonomy and decisions about contact with outsiders.Rosolie has discussed these challenges in interviews, including the difficult questions surrounding how outsiders should respond to the needs of isolated communities. Such issues require careful, rights-based approaches and consultation with appropriate Indigenous representatives and specialists.Funding helps keep rangers in the forestConservation in remote rainforest is expensive, and Junglekeepers relies on donations and fundraising to sustain its operations.In December 2022, Age of Union Alliance, the environmental organisation founded by entrepreneur Dax Dasilva, announced a five-year commitment of $3.5 million to Junglekeepers. The announcement followed an earlier investment of $625,000 in 2021.Junglekeepers' March 2025 announcement about its 2024 annual report said the organisation had raised $3.3 million during that year, a 469% increase compared with 2023. It also reported that 20% of donations were recurring.These figures refer to different funding announcements and reporting periods, so they should not automatically be added together as though they represent separate, unrestricted funds available to the organisation today.The money supports the practical work of conservation, from paying rangers and maintaining boats to buying land and monitoring threats. Sustained funding is especially important when conservation teams operate in remote locations where transport, communication and emergency support can be difficult to arrange.Why protecting the Las Piedras corridor mattersThe Las Piedras watershed forms part of the wider Andes-Amazon region, where the Andes and Amazon ecosystems meet. This broader landscape is recognised for its exceptional biodiversity, and its forests provide habitat for numerous species.Junglekeepers says wildlife recorded in the area includes hundreds of bird species, several kinds of monkeys and threatened animals such as jaguars, giant otters and harpy eagles. The organisation has also described using camera traps and other monitoring tools to observe wildlife and detect forest fires.These activities can help conservation teams understand what is happening in the forest and respond to emerging threats. However, the presence of wildlife or the use of monitoring equipment alone does not establish that a particular species' population is increasing because of the organisation's work. Demonstrating that would require comparable data collected over time.The broader conservation goal is to keep large areas of connected forest intact. Fragmentation can isolate wildlife populations, while roads and extractive activities can bring further pressure to ecosystems that have remained relatively remote.A two-decade effort with a much larger goal aheadFor Rosolie, the work has developed from a young explorer's fascination with the Amazon into a long-term commitment to conservation. His experience also illustrates how protecting a forest can require years of relationship-building, local partnerships, fundraising and repeated efforts to respond to new threats.Junglekeepers' reported protection of almost 160,000 acres represents a substantial conservation footprint, but the organisation's longer-term target is approximately 300,000 acres. Reaching that goal will require continued funding, cooperation with local communities and effective responses to illegal activities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK govt announces new ‘safe and legal’ routes for refugees in India to resettle in UK
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from London: In a bid to dissuade asylum-seekers from arriving in Britain on the backs of lorries or via small boats, the UK home office
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: In a bid to dissuade asylum-seekers from arriving in Britain on the backs of lorries or via small boats, the UK home office has announced three new “safe and legal” sponsorship routes for refugees in India and six other countries to come to the UK and claim asylum.The new routes are initially targeted at refugees who have sought protection in India, Bangladesh, Egypt, Kenya, Malaysia, Pakistan and Uganda.To be eligible, the refugees will need to be outside their country of nationality, to have been verified by the UNHCR as meeting the definition of refugee and to have registered with the UNHCR or relevant authorities in one of these seven countries before Oct 1. So, in India’s case, it could be Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Afghans, Rohingya and others from Myanmar, who could be eligible for these routes, but not Indian nationals residing in India, nor internally displaced people.The refugee sponsorship routes, modelled on a similar programme in Canada, allow sponsors in the UK to identify refugees they wish to sponsor. The new routes are named community sponsorship, which enables UK charities to identify refugees they wish to sponsor; refugee work, which enables UK employers to sponsor and provide refugees jobs; and refugee study, which enables UK universities to sponsor refugees to study in the UK. Once resettled, the refugees will have an immediate right to work, study and to access welfare benefits in Britain and be placed on a five-year path to permanent resettlement.Sponsors will have to finance and provide their accommodation, the aim being to reduce the amount UK’s govt spends on asylum hotels.Applications to be sponsors for the community and study route have opened and the first arrivals are expected in autumn 2027. Applications under the work route will open in spring 2027.Both Reform UK and the Conservatives vowed to shut the scheme if they come to power. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said until illegal migration is stopped, “we should not be creating new routes into the UK for asylum claimants”.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
